title: Moses' Birth
summary: Exodus 2 tells how Moses survives Pharaoh's order to kill Hebrew boys. His mother hides him for three months, then places him in a basket among the reeds by the river while his sister watches. Pharaoh's daughter finds the child and, after his sister intervenes, arranges for a Hebrew woman to nurse him. The child returns to the princess and is raised as her son. The story centers on several women's actions that protect a vulnerable child in the middle of state violence.
historical_context: The narrative situates Moses' birth within Pharaoh's campaign against the growing Hebrew population. It names the family only as Levites and presents the Nile riverbank, the basket, and Pharaoh's household as the settings for the rescue. These are details of the biblical account; the sources listed here do not independently identify the Pharaoh or verify the episode historically.
literary_context: The birth story follows Pharaoh's escalating attempt to control Israel's growth. His order is resisted first by the midwives and then, in this episode, by Moses' mother, sister, and Pharaoh's daughter. The repeated movement between the riverbank and Pharaoh's household turns the ruler's own home into the place where the threatened child is preserved. The narrative does not yet explain how Moses will lead Israel; it leaves that development for later chapters.
covenantal_significance: The child survives because several people act to preserve his life, even within the household of the ruler who ordered the deaths. The passage does not present the rescue as a simple escape from oppression: Moses grows up under Pharaoh's roof while the Hebrew people remain enslaved. It begins the story of the future deliverer, but keeps the suffering of the community in view rather than treating one child's survival as the end of their hardship.
canonical_role: The account introduces Moses as a child spared from Pharaoh's violence and raised in the royal household. That unusual beginning prepares for the adult Moses who will later confront Pharaoh and lead Israel out of Egypt. The story therefore links the opening oppression narrative to the deliverance that follows, while making clear that rescue has begun for Moses before it has come to the people as a whole.

interpretive_notes.note: The Exodus is both historical rescue and theological pattern.
Later biblical texts frequently reuse Exodus language for salvation and return.
